displayQuote: No snowflake in an avalanche ever feels responsible

meta.title: Who really said "No snowflake in an avalanche ever feels responsible"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Voltaire — that credit first shows up in a 2004 meditation book, 226 years after he died. The line belongs to the Polish aphorist Stanisław Jerzy Lec, printed in the 1968 translation More Unkempt Thoughts. The Polish original has never been found.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No snowflake in an avalanche ever feels responsible'?
meta.ogDescription: Voltaire is out by two centuries. It is Stanisław Jerzy Lec's — on the strength of a 1968 English translation whose Polish original nobody has yet located.

answer.label: Stanisław Jerzy Lec — but only in English so far
answer.sourceLine: Voltaire has no connection to it whatsoever: the earliest Voltaire credit anyone has found is a 2004 popular meditation anthology, 226 years after his death. The line belongs to Stanisław Jerzy Lec, and it is printed in More Unkempt Thoughts (Funk & Wagnalls, 1968), translated from Polish by Jacek Galazka. There is one loose thread we will not tuck in: nobody has located the Polish original, and the earliest English instance of all — a Paul Harvey column of January 1964 — carries no attribution at all.

source.excerpt: No snowflake in an avalanche ever feels responsible.
trail: The earliest instance of the thought in English is 9 January 1964, in a Paul Harvey newspaper column, in a slightly different shape: ‘In an avalanche, no one snowflake ever feels responsible.’ No author is named the chronology ↗.

Six weeks later, in February 1964, a Missouri newspaper printed the now-familiar wording in a column of quotations compiled by high-school students, credited to ‘Etaislaw Lee’ — almost certainly a mangling of Stanislaw Lec. That garbled name is the first sighting of the real author.

In 1968 the line appears properly in print, in More Unkempt Thoughts, Lec’s aphorisms Englished by Jacek Galazka for Funk & Wagnalls. That is the anchor citation, and it is the reason the attribution stands.

The Polish is the gap. Researchers have checked the 1964 and 1966 editions of Lec’s Myśli nieuczesane nowe — the obvious candidate — and the aphorism is not in them. A Polish wording circulates online (‘Żaden płatek śniegu nie czuje się odpowiedzialny za lawinę’), but it is crowd-sourced, unverified, and reads like a back-translation. We are not presenting it as the original.
source.excerptNote: Galazka’s English, as printed in 1968. It is a whole moral argument in nine words: an avalanche is made of nothing but snowflakes, and yet responsibility divides by the number of participants until it rounds to zero.

source.rightsNote: Treat this one as in copyright on both sides. Lec died in 1966, so his Polish text runs to about 2037 in the EU under life-plus-seventy. The English you actually see is Jacek Galazka’s translation, published in 1968, and a translation is its own copyrightable work with its own term — so even the day the Polish falls out of copyright, this wording will not. Quote the sentence with attribution, as here; do not treat it as free stock text. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Voltaire
author.metaLine: 1694–1778 · French Enlightenment writer, satirist and philosopher
author.bio: Voltaire is the default owner of any homeless epigram in English, and this one reached him by a comic route. Watch the name decay: ‘Etaislaw Lee’ in 1964, then Stanislaus Leszczynski — an actual eighteenth-century king of Poland — in a 1973 jeweller’s advertisement, then the novelist Stanislaw Lem in a 1997 quotation dictionary, and finally, in a 2004 meditation anthology, Voltaire. An aphorism with an unpronounceable author drifts toward the most famous aphorist available. He is also credited, wrongly, with ‘I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it’ — written about him by his biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall in 1906.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This line has been handed to five different people, and four of the five errors come from the same cause: nobody in the English-speaking press could spell ‘Stanisław Jerzy Lec.’

items.why: The earliest located Voltaire ascription is a 2004 compilation, 1,001 Meditations by Mike George. Nothing of the kind appears in Voltaire’s French. The French version now in circulation reads like a translation from the English rather than an eighteenth-century original the trail ↗.
A 1973 Pennsylvania newspaper advertisement credited ‘Stanislaus Leszczynski,’ the eighteenth-century King of Poland. He shares a first name with Lec and nothing else. Unsupported.
Simpson’s Contemporary Quotations (1997) credited the science-fiction novelist Stanisław Lem — while citing More Unkempt Thoughts, which is Lec’s book. The citation was right; the name was misread.
A 2006 Reader’s Digest anthology gave it to the comedian. By then the saying had been in print for forty years.

items.scope: The honest gap in the Lec case
items.why: The attribution rests on a 1968 English translation. Researchers who read Polish have checked the likeliest source volumes and not found it, and the very earliest English instance — January 1964 — names nobody. So Lec is the best-supported author, not a proven one. We would rather say that than pretend.

misattribution.truthLine: Stanisław Jerzy Lec, on the strength of More Unkempt Thoughts (1968) in Jacek Galazka’s translation. Voltaire is unsupported, and the Polish original remains unlocated the investigation ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It names something that has no good name: the arithmetic by which a crowd commits a thing that none of its members would commit. Everyone in the avalanche is doing exactly what the snowflake next to them is doing, which feels, from the inside, like doing nothing at all.

It also matters who wrote it. Lec was a Polish Jew who survived a Nazi labour camp, escaped a grave he had been made to dig, and then lived out his life under a regime that ran on ordinary people going along. His aphorisms are short because saying more was dangerous, and this one is about the machinery he watched from inside.
detailsBody: January 1964: Paul Harvey’s column prints the thought with no author at all.
February 1964: a Missouri high-school column credits ‘Etaislaw Lee’ — a garbled Stanislaw Lec.
1968: More Unkempt Thoughts, translated by Jacek Galazka, prints it properly under Lec’s name.
1970: a syndicated columnist prints a variant credited to ‘Stanislaw J. Lee.’
1973: a jeweller’s advertisement credits King Stanislaus Leszczynski.
1997: a quotation dictionary credits Stanislaw Lem, while citing Lec’s book.
2004: a meditation anthology credits Voltaire, and that is the version the internet kept.
context.pull: Four wrong authors in forty years, and every one of them starts with the letters S-t-a-n.
